title: Quadratic Taylor: A Plane Curves Into a Bowl
topic: Two-variable Taylor expansion to second order. The tangent plane (order 1) matches value + slopes; adding the Hessian quadratic form (order 2) matches curvature. As a sweep moves from order 0 → 1 → 2 the approximation surface fits the underlying function visibly tighter and the residual |f − T_k| collapses.

beats.narration: The tangent plane gets the slope right. To get the curvature right, add the Hessian.

elements.content: Plane catches slope. Bowl catches curvature.

beats.narration: Start in one variable. Pick a point. The constant approximation just holds f of a. The linear one adds the slope. The quadratic one adds one half f double prime, and the curve and the parabola lock together at the point.

elements.content: Curve f(x) in violet, marker at point a
Order 1: tangent line f(a)+f'(a)(x−a) in amber
Order 2: parabola adding ½f''(a)(x−a)² in rose

beats.narration: In two variables, replace the slope with the gradient and replace the second derivative with the Hessian matrix. The quadratic term reads h transpose H h over two, where h is the displacement from the centre.

elements.content: T₂(x, y) = f(a, b) + ∇f(a,b)·h + ½ hᵀ H(a,b) h
value · slopes · curvatures — all locked in at (a, b)

beats.narration: Pick a saddle-shaped surface and watch the approximation snap into focus. Order zero is flat. Order one tilts the plane to match the gradient — already much better. Order two adds the Hessian bowl, and the surface and the approximation hug the centre.

elements.content: 3D-style projected wireframe of f(x,y) at base
Sliced cross-section of f and T_k across the diagonal (genuine value-driven motion)
Order indicator k = 0, 1, 2 — stepped over time
Live residual bar |f − T_k| at the sample displacement

beats.narration: First order locks in slope. Second order locks in curvature. That is why the Hessian decides whether a critical point is a hill, a hollow, or a saddle.
